title: The Bala tradition
hookLine: a popular tradition tells the stories through Bhai Bala, a companion historians discuss

cards: "I was there." Three words, and listeners lean in. A story told by a stranger is information.
A story told by someone who walked the road beside the hero is something else: you can hear the dust on their shoes.

Some Sikh homes have a painting of Guru Nanak seated with two companions: Bhai Mardana with his rabab, and a second man, Bhai Bala. That second figure belongs to a whole family of janamsakhis told in his voice.

teach.h: BALA TELLS GURU ANGAD WHAT HE SAW.
teach.b: Here's how the Bala janamsakhis present themselves. Bhai Bala, a companion of Guru Nanak on his travels, sits with the second Guru, Guru Angad, and tells what he saw. The stories come in that frame: told by a friend.
It's a warm frame, and the Bala tellings are popular.
They're fuller than the Puratan stories, with more detail, more conversation, and more wonders.

Now the careful part, because historians discuss Bala. They ask whether a companion named Bala was really with Nanak on his travels. Some think the frame was added later, to give the stories a witness.
Others keep the question open. Sikhs differ on this too. Some hold Bhai Bala dear as a real companion.

Others read the Bala janamsakhis with more caution, and prefer older tellings for history. Both take Guru Nanak seriously; they're asking different questions of the same stories. So what can we say for sure?
That the frame matters. A story told as if by a friend asks to be trusted the way you trust a friend.

teach.h: A FRIEND'S VOICE IS A GIFT AND A TRUST.
teach.b: That's a gift, and also a responsibility, because a friend's voice can carry things that grew later.
The Bala tradition shows how a telling gets its warmth. Yesterday's shows how a telling stays close to the stone. Sikh readers have kept both.

how: Some Sikh homes and gurdwaras display paintings of Guru Nanak with Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, and sakhis from the Bala tradition are still retold, while historians read them alongside older tellings.

o: a companion in whose voice stories are told
a child's name for the young Guru Nanak

games.q: the Bala telling — tap the pairs.

s: historians agree Bala was with Nanak on every journey
historians discuss whether he was there at all; some think the frame came later.
the Bala stories are framed as Bala telling Guru Angad what he saw
that's the frame: told by a friend.

games.q: you love a story told in a friend's voice, but a historian says the friend may not have been there. what do you do?
o: keep the story, and hold the question honestly.
games.why: Sikhs differ on Bhai Bala: some hold him dear as a real companion, others read his tellings with caution. both take the stories seriously.

practice: Bring back a story you heard as a child, from a parent, grandparent, teacher or older cousin, and hear it first in their voice, the way they told it.
Notice what their voice added, the pauses, the warmth, the bits they lingered on: some of that is the best part, and some of it might not be history, so hold both without throwing either away.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the person who told it to you.

wordCard.voice: Bala, the companion in whose voice the Bala janamsakhis are told, his place in Nanak's travels still discussed by historians.

orig.note: sakhi: one story of the Guru's life, the unit every janamsakhi is built from.

carryVoice: Your line: told by a friend. A friend's voice is a gift and a trust. Until next time.
